questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name the moves in a short paragraph
questions.stem: This paragraph runs: "The archive opened in 1974 and was catalogued by hand. The first catalogue listed 3,200 boxes. A 1998 spot check found 900 of them were unlisted. This paragraph sets up, quantifies, tests, and then interprets, and the last move is the load-bearing one because without it the paragraph is a set of numbers. The tempting reading names the topics instead, dates and box counts, which is what the paragraph is about rather than what it does; aboutness is not a move, and a list of subjects cannot be checked against the order of the sentences.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name three moves in a paragraph and say what each depends on
questions.stem: This paragraph runs: "Nobody expected the scheme to work, least of all the committee. It has now been running for six years, and the waiting list has fallen by half. Here the reversal of expectation enables the reading of the figures, and the figures make the silence worth reporting. The tempting reading names the paragraph's subjects instead, a committee, a scheme, a waiting list, which is what the paragraph is about; a description of moves has to keep asking what each sentence is doing, and aboutness never changes from one sentence to the next.

questions.learningObjective: identify what a dangling modifier attaches to
questions.stem: In "The council promised a reply to residents still waiting for the results," which noun does the phrase after the comma attach to?

options.text: To the results, so the sentence says the results are still waiting
To the council, so the council is still waiting for results
options.misconception: attaches the phrase to the wrong party in the sentence

options.text: To the promise, so the promise has not yet been made
options.misconception: reads the phrase as a comment on the earlier noun

options.text: To nothing, since a phrase after a comma is always a new sentence
options.misconception: treats the comma as a sentence boundary

questions.explanation: A phrase that follows the noun it describes attaches to the nearest available noun, which here is results, and the sentence therefore says the results are waiting rather than the residents. That is why the revision moves the phrase up: 'residents who are still waiting for the results' leaves nothing to attach to but residents. The tempting reading looks for a natural intention and assigns the phrase to the council or the promise, but a reader takes the sentence as written, and the writer's intention is not available to them unless the sentence is fixed.
questions.hint: Ask which noun sits nearest the phrase.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a sentence to restore parallelism
questions.stem: For the purpose of making the list parallel, which revision of "The scheme reduced waiting times, cut costs, and there were fewer complaints" is correct?

options.text: It reduced waiting times, it cut costs, and it reduced complaints
The scheme reduced waiting times and costs, with fewer complaints
options.misconception: merges two items into one and drops the third verb

options.text: Reduced waiting times, cut costs, and fewer complaints were the results
options.misconception: leaves the list without a subject to belong to

options.text: The scheme reduced waiting times, cut costs, and complaints fell
options.misconception: keeps the third item in a different grammatical form

questions.explanation: A list is parallel when each item is the same kind of thing, and three items each with their own verb and object lets a reader take the three results in one breath. The original mixes two verbs with a noun phrase, which makes the third item arrive under a different grammar and quietly changes its status. The tempting reading thinks shortening is the same as parallelising, as in B, and it is a genuine improvement in length; but the third result is now a consequence floating in a prepositional phrase instead of an action the scheme took, and that is a change of claim, not of form.
questions.hint: Ask whether each item can be read the same way as the first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a sentence so its claim fits its evidence
questions.stem: A draft says, "The scheme has proved that early intervention prevents hospital admissions." The evidence is a single district over two years, with no comparison group. What revision fits the evidence?

options.text: "Early intervention is associated with fewer admissions in the district studied"
"The scheme has shown how effective early intervention can be"
options.misconception: keeps the strong verb and adds praise instead of evidence

options.text: "Hospital admissions fell after the scheme, and the fall was large"
options.misconception: retains an unmeasured size and an implied sequence

options.text: "Further study will confirm that early intervention prevents admissions"
options.misconception: keeps the causal claim and postpones the test

questions.explanation: A claim should be no stronger than the design behind it, and one district with no comparison group supports a relationship observed in one place, not a prevention established in general. A says exactly that, and the word associated is the price of accuracy here. The tempting reading likes C, which is concrete and gives a direction; but 'large' is a size nobody measured and 'after' is doing causal work in a study that cannot show cause, and D simply schedules the strong claim for a future hearing, which is the same claim with a delay on it.
questions.hint: Ask what the design can show and what it cannot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: select the revisions that preserve the claim while tightening it
questions.stem: A reviewer proposes four cuts to a sentence. Three keep the claim and the evidence it rests on. Which three?

options.text: Delete 'in the second report of the year', which dates a source already given
Delete 'appears to', which makes a measured claim sound certain
options.misconception: removes the calibration and keeps the assertion

options.text: Delete 'very', which intensifies a word that carries no figure
Delete 'according to the district's own figures', which names the source
Delete 'because the count was taken at the door', which explains the measure
options.misconception: keeps the deletion that takes away what the count is

questions.explanation: A cut is safe when the deleted words add nothing a reader needs: a second date for a source already identified, an intensifier in front of a word carrying no figure, and a redundant label for material the paragraph has already attributed. B and E are the two cuts that change what the sentence claims, by making a hedged finding sound certain and by removing the explanation of how the count was taken. The tempting reading counts length, and both B and E are short, which is exactly why they are the tempting ones.
questions.hint: Ask which deletions change what the sentence asserts.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify which verb agrees with the true subject across an intervening phrase
questions.stem: In "The list of damaged files sent to the council has been ignored for a year," which verb agrees with the subject?

options.text: Has, because the subject is the list
Have, because files are also mentioned in the sentence
options.misconception: takes the nearest plural as the subject

options.text: Have, because the files were sent and the list was not
options.misconception: redistributes the grammatical role of the phrase

options.text: Has, because the council is the party that ignored it
options.misconception: gives the agreement to the agent of the ignoring

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject of the sentence, and here the subject is the head of the subject phrase, which is list; everything between the article and the head is a modifier, and a long modifier does not change who the sentence is about. The tempting reading follows the nearest plural, and proximity is a genuine problem in English, which is why a writer can reduce the ambiguity by moving the phrase; but the rule is about the head, and 'the list of files' is one thing and not several.
questions.hint: Ask which noun the sentence is about rather than mentioning.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a sentence to remove ambiguous pronoun reference
questions.stem: For the purpose of removing ambiguity, which revision of "The survey told the council that it would fall" is correct?

options.text: The survey told the council that the figure would fall
The council told the survey that it would fall
options.misconception: reverses the reporters and the reported

options.text: It told the council that the figure would fall
options.misconception: leaves the first pronoun as the only reference available

options.text: The survey told it that the figure would fall
options.misconception: removes the council and leaves the pronoun still ambiguous

questions.explanation: A pronoun whose referent is genuinely available in two places has to go, and here it can be the survey, which reported a fall, or the council, which is the party that might have been told it would fall. Replacing it with the noun the sentence is about makes the claim unambiguous without changing a word of the substance. The tempting reading keeps a pronoun because prose likes them, and C does replace the later one; but it leaves the first untouched, so the sentence can still be read two ways and the ambiguity has been moved rather than closed.
questions.hint: Ask how many things in the sentence the pronoun could mean.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a sentence to put the action in a verb
questions.stem: A sentence reads, "The implementation of the scheme took place in June, and the evaluation of it was completed in March." For the purpose of making the actions visible, what is the key repair?

options.text: Put a verb in the subject of each clause, naming who acted
Add a second noun to each abstract term, to make it heavier
options.misconception: mistakes added weight for added clarity

options.text: Move both dates to the front of the sentence, so they lead
options.misconception: reorders the sentence while leaving the actions abstract

options.text: Replace the abstract nouns with the word 'process', which names both
options.misconception: substitutes one vague noun for two and loses the distinction

questions.explanation: An abstract noun in the subject slot hides the actor, because nothing in 'the implementation of the scheme' says who did anything; a verb restores it, and in these two clauses it also restores the difference between doing the scheme and judging it, which a reader would otherwise lose behind a pair of similar abstractions. The tempting reading treats weight as clarity, and heavier nouns feel more formal; but a reader cannot see an action inside a noun, and moving the dates to the front leaves the sentence's shape intact while leaving the sentence's content as invisible as it was.
questions.hint: Ask which words tell the reader who did what.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a concession so that it actually concedes something
questions.stem: A writer's concession currently concedes nothing: "Although some people may have concerns about the new hours, those concerns are entirely unfounded." Explain what a real concession would have to concede, and what the revision must not do.

answer.exemplar: It has to grant the concern as reasonable on its face, saying that the hours are harder to reach for people on early shifts, which is true and which the writer can grant without giving up the case. It must not name who holds the concern, because a concession that identifies a group turns into an objection the writer then has to defeat, and it must not concede any fact about the hours, since nothing in the writer's case requires that.

questions.explanation: A concession that is immediately cancelled is not a concession, and readers notice the cancellation, which makes the whole sentence read as a formality and the concerns beneath it as unconsidered. A real concession admits something a person who disagreed could accept as a starting point, and here that is the difficulty of the change for early-shift workers. The tempting reading makes the concession dramatic instead, by naming a loud opponent and dismissing them, which produces a stronger-feeling sentence and no admission at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a person who disagreed could accept as true.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: order claims from most to least supported
questions.stem: A draft makes four claims in one paragraph. Place them from the one that asserts least beyond its evidence to the one that asserts most.

options.text: The two-signature rule was therefore theatre
options.misconception: treats a verdict about intent as needing no evidence of intent at all

options.text: The 1994 notice required two signatures before a payment was released
options.misconception: puts a record's own wording behind a judgment nothing in the file supports

options.text: The largest of those payments was 40 per cent of the year's spending
options.misconception: reads a proportion of a total as though the total were already given

options.text: Between 1996 and 2000, three payments were released with one signature
options.misconception: reverses the count and the rule, so the compliance claim comes before the record of it

questions.explanation: Each claim here adds a new demand on the evidence, so the order runs from the claim that asks least to the one that asks most. B reports what a document says and nothing else; D adds a count and a period, which needs the payment records; C adds a proportion, which needs both that count and the year's total; and A adds a judgment about what the rule was for, which needs all three plus a view of intent. The tempting reading puts the verdict first because a verdict is what a paragraph is for, but a claim that asserts least beyond its evidence is not the same as the claim a writer would most like to make, and ordering by preference is how the weakest sentence ends up carrying the most.
questions.hint: Ask what each claim needs beyond the one before it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a sentence so its tense matches the reported sequence
questions.stem: A report says, "The 1994 review said the scheme was unworkable. Two years later, the same committee says it proved excellent." Which reading of the tenses is right?

options.text: Both are reported speech, so past tense inside is correct in each
Only the first is reported speech, since the second is the writer's own view
options.misconception: assumes the writer endorses the committee's later judgment

options.text: The second should be in present tense, since it is the current finding
options.misconception: ignores that the sentence reports what a body said

options.text: Both should be in quotation marks, since tense cannot report speech
options.misconception: mistakes a punctuation convention for a tense rule

questions.explanation: A reporting verb in the past tense carries reported speech into the past, so a review saying in 1994 that the scheme was unworkable is reported in the past in both halves, and a committee saying two years later that it proved excellent is reported the same way. The tense is not the writer's position at all. The tempting reading treats the second clause as present-day fact, since a reader may well prefer it, but the writer has reported what a body said and has not said which of them is right, and switching the tense would smuggle in a judgment the sentence deliberately withholds.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking in each half of the sentence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the clash in a sentence that mixes two images
questions.stem: A sentence reads, "The proposal was a runaway success that the committee put a brake on." What is the state of that sentence?

options.text: Vivid, since success and braking belong to the same kind of world
options.misconception: assumes a shared world of money and vehicles

options.text: Clashing, since the two images belong to different systems of thought
Informal, which is why it does not suit a committee report
options.misconception: reduces a clash of images to a matter of tone

options.text: Figurative, which is a category on its own and needs no repair
options.misconception: declines to assess a clash that a reader will notice at once

questions.explanation: A metaphor imports a whole system of implications, and two systems imported into one sentence pull against each other: success runs away in one direction, brakes slow in the other, and the reader spends effort reconciling images that were never in the same world. The sentence is not vague, it is busy, and busy is the failure a reader notices first. The tempting reading finds the image vivid, and taken alone either image is; the trouble is that they are doing different jobs, and vividness is a property of one image at a time.
questions.hint: Ask what each image implies beyond the words it contains.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: select the revisions that weaken what the sentence claims
questions.stem: A writer offers four revisions of one sentence. Three of them weaken the claim. Which three?

options.text: Change 'proved' to 'suggested', which fits the size of the study
options.misconception: matches the claim to the evidence rather than weakening it

options.text: Add 'in two schools', which narrows the claim to what was seen
Add 'the committee thinks', which attributes the judgment to a source
Replace 'cuts' with 'might cut', which makes the effect conditional
Delete 'last year', since the date is given in the previous sentence
options.misconception: removes a repetition rather than a claim

questions.explanation: A revision weakens a claim when it hands the claim to someone else, confines it to a smaller set of cases, or makes it merely possible; B, C, and D do those three things, and a reader who wanted the strong version has lost it. A matches the verb to the size of the study, which is a repair rather than a loss, and E removes a repetition. The tempting reading treats every softening word as a loss, which would make precision impossible, since a claim that overstates its evidence has to be reduced for the paragraph to be worth anything.
questions.hint: Ask which revisions keep the writer as the one claiming.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify when a passive must become active
questions.stem: A sentence reads, "The report was commissioned by the residents' association, which was not consulted until the draft was finished." For the purpose of making the failure visible, what must change?

options.text: The second clause must name the association, since the agent is the point
The first clause must become passive, so both halves match
options.misconception: reverses the repair and loses the agent entirely

options.text: The verb 'was commissioned' must stay, since it is the accurate tense
options.misconception: confuses a voice choice with a tense choice

options.text: The relative pronoun must be removed, since it weakens the clause
options.misconception: changes grammar while leaving the failure unstated

questions.explanation: The sentence buries the association in a relative clause, and the association is the whole point: the readers who asked for the report were not asked what was in it. Putting the agent where the verb is makes the sequence of events readable as a sequence, commission then non-consultation, instead of a stray note at the end. The tempting reading asks for grammatical tidiness, matching the two clauses or tidying the pronoun; but a sentence can be perfectly balanced and still hide the thing the writer needed a reader to see, and tidiness is a property of the frame, not of what the frame shows.
questions.hint: Ask who is the agent of the failure the sentence describes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: correct a figure that has been misreported
questions.stem: A source says the scheme saved "£40,000 a year." A draft writes, "The scheme has saved £40,000 since 2016." For the purpose of accuracy, what is the correction?

options.text: Restore 'a year', since the source reports an annual rate and not a total
Change the figure to £400,000, since ten years at the rate gives that total
options.misconception: does the arithmetic the source never asked for and asserts a total

options.text: Delete the figure, since figures in sources are unreliable in general
options.misconception: throws out a number for a fault in one unit

options.text: Change 'saved' to 'was expected to save', since reports are forecasts
options.misconception: recasts a recorded rate as a projection

questions.explanation: The source reports a rate, and a rate and a total are different quantities, so the draft has changed what the number means by changing its noun; the correction is a word, and it makes the sentence say what the source said. The tempting reading wants a bigger number, on the reasonable ground that ten years should be worth more than one; but multiplying a rate by a period is a calculation the writer may do, not a figure the source supports, and presenting the product as though it were reported would be the same error in a larger figure.
questions.hint: Ask whether the source gave a rate or a total.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: revise a claim so its wording matches the size of its evidence
questions.stem: A paragraph reports 312 complaints in 2019 and 61 in 2023, and concludes, "Complaints collapsed, which proves the new process works." For the purpose of matching the claim to the evidence, which revision is right?

options.text: "Complaints fell sharply, and the new process is the likeliest reason"
"Complaints collapsed, though the new process may not be the reason"
options.misconception: keeps the strong word and negates the claim instead of replacing it

options.text: "The new process works, since complaints fell while it was in place"
options.misconception: keeps the verdict and makes the timing its evidence

options.text: "Complaints fell 80 per cent, which is a result worth noting"
options.misconception: keeps the figure and declines to say what it shows

questions.explanation: The numbers support a large fall and nothing more, so the sentence should say that the fall is large and that the new process is the likeliest explanation, which is a prediction a reader can test rather than a proof nobody can check. That revision keeps both the finding and the writer's interest in it. The tempting reading prefers C, which sounds like a stronger sentence; but a fall that happened while a process was in place is a fact about timing, and treating timing as proof is the same step the original made, now with a softer word in front of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the two numbers establish and what they suggest.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain how to test a revision against its stated purpose
questions.stem: A student rewrites a sentence for economy and then a second sentence for precision, and cannot tell whether either rewrite worked. Explain how the student can test each rewrite against the purpose it was given.

answer.exemplar: For the economy rewrite, the test is whether the claim, the evidence, and the limit on it all survived; if any one of the three is gone, the sentence is shorter and no longer says what it said. For the precision rewrite, the test is whether a reader could now go and check the claim, which means a count, a date, or an occasion has replaced whatever was standing in for one. The student should state the purpose in a sentence before rewriting, because a purpose held in the head is easy to lose halfway through an edit.

questions.explanation: A revision is judged by the purpose it was given, and the purpose has to be written down, because a rewrite that is going well feels like improvement and feels the same whether it is improving precision or merely shortening. The economy test asks what survived, the precision test asks what a reader could now check, and neither can be run from memory of the original. The tempting reading tests a rewrite by whether it reads better, which is the one measure that cannot fail; a sentence can be much prettier and have lost the limit that made it honest.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could do with the new sentence that they could not do before.
